extracted.intended_audience: higher-education professionals and K–12 educators (admissions officers, faculty, and test-prep instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and scoring rubric for the redesigned SAT Essay: what it measures, the common prompt/task, how source texts are selected, and the three scored dimensions (Reading, Analysis, Writing) including score-band descriptors and scoring procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall purpose of the SAT Essay
rubrics_metrics.description: The SAT Essay assesses whether students can comprehend an appropriately challenging source text and craft an effective written analysis, supported by critical reasoning and evidence drawn from the source text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assessment departs from eliciting subjective opinions; the task requires objective analysis of how the author builds an argument. The Essay reports three separate scores (reading, analysis, writing). The task uses a common prompt across administrations and varies only by source text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common prompt / task instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: As you read the passage below, consider how [author] uses evidence, reasoning, and stylistic or persuasive elements to build an argument. Write an essay explaining how [author] builds an argument to persuade the audience that [insert claim].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In your essay, analyze how the author uses one or more listed features (or features of your own choice) to strengthen the logic and persuasiveness of the argument. Be sure analysis focuses on the most relevant features. Do not explain whether you agree with the author’s claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source text selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages present arguments that examine ideas, debates, and trends across arts, sciences, and civic/cultural/political life; they have wide interest and accessibility and convey nuanced views on complex subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All passages are taken from high-quality, previously published sources, ~650–750 words in length, with complexity appropriate for high school students. Prior knowledge of the passage topic is not expected or required. Texts are selected for use of evidence, reasoning, and/or stylistic and persuasive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading (scored dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures demonstrated comprehension of the source text: understanding of central idea(s) and important details; correctness of interpretation; and appropriate use of textual evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension scored 2–8 (two raters give 1–4, then summed/doubled rules apply). Score-band descriptors: • Weak (reader score 1): little/no comprehension, may include only details without reference to central ideas, makes little/no use of textual evidence. • Fair (2): some comprehension of central idea(s) but not important details; limited/haphazard use of textual evidence; may contain errors of fact/interpretation. • Good (3): effective comprehension of central ideas and important details; appropriate use of textual evidence; free of substantive errors. • Excellent (4): thorough/comprehensive understanding; skillful use of textual evidence; free of errors of fact/interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis (scored dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures the quality of analysis of the source text: discerning which features of the passage (e.g., use of evidence, reasoning, stylistic/persuasive elements) are most relevant and explaining how those features help build the author’s argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension scored 2–8. Score-band descriptors: • Weak (1): offers little/no discernible or effective analysis and may be largely summary. • Fair (2): identifies aspects of author’s use of evidence/reasoning/style without explanation or offers limited analysis and partial understanding; contains little/relevant support. • Good (3): offers an effective analysis and demonstrates understanding of the analytic task; competently evaluates author’s use of evidence/reasoning/style; contains relevant and sufficient support. • Excellent (4): offers insightful, thorough evaluation demonstrating sophisticated understanding; contains relevant, sufficient, and strategically chosen support; consistently focuses on features most relevant to the task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing (scored dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures quality of writing: presence of a central claim; cohesion (effective introduction/conclusion and clear progression of ideas); sentence variety; precise word choice; style/tone; and control of conventions of Standard Written English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension scored 2–8. Score-band descriptors: • Weak (1): little/no cohesion, inadequate control of language, lacks recognizable introduction/conclusion, poor progression of ideas, weak control of conventions with numerous errors. • Fair (2): limited cohesion, some progression but not throughout, limited sentence variety and vague word choice, errors that detract from quality and may impede understanding. • Good (3): mostly cohesive with effective use/control of language, effective introduction/conclusion, variety in sentence structures, precise word choice, maintains formal/objective tone, good control of conventions and free of significant errors. • Excellent (4): cohesive and highly effective command of language, skillful introduction/conclusion, deliberate progression of ideas, wide variety of sentence structures, consistent precise word choice, strong command of conventions and virtually free of errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of textual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Test takers must make purposeful, substantive use of textual evidence (quotations, paraphrases, or both) to support interpretation and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher-scoring responses make skillful and strategically chosen use of textual evidence demonstrating comprehensive understanding. Lower-scoring responses make limited/haphazard or little/no use of evidence. Evidence should be relevant and sufficient to support claims and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on relevant features and sufficiency of support
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses should focus on features of the text that are most relevant to addressing the task and provide relevant, sufficient support for claims or points made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower scores reflect a lack of focus on relevant features or insufficient/irrelevant support. High scores reflect consistent focus on relevant features and relevant, sufficient, and strategically chosen support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring procedure and score computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each essay is read by two trained raters who award 1–4 points for each dimension. If raters’ scores are the same or within one point, the scores are added (yielding 2–8). If raters’ scores differ by more than one point on any dimension, a third, senior rater scores that dimension and that senior score is doubled to yield the 2–8 dimension score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension scores range 2–8; Total Essay Score is the sum of Reading + Analysis + Writing (range 6–24). Essay scores are reported separately from the SAT total score. Raters are trained to hold every student to the same standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and use of scores
rubrics_metrics.description: The three separate scores provide targeted information about student achievement and can inform instruction, placement, and advising; a single total score may obscure differences in performance across dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colleges can use dimension scores (and percentile tables based on total essay score) to evaluate overall performance and identify specific strengths/weaknesses (e.g., high Reading and Writing but low Analysis indicates targeted instruction on analytic skills). Institutions can run placement/validity studies (e.g., via ACES) to relate SAT Essay scores to course grades and placement decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity and alignment with postsecondary writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence shows the SAT Essay aligns with analytical writing required in postsecondary settings and has strong content validity (face and curricular validity) based on expert input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although early pilot predictive studies didn’t include the Essay, the College Board intends ongoing validity research; institutions are encouraged to examine the relationship between Essay scores and college writing outcomes using ACES.
